text: A [[cyclone|cyclone]] is a giant spinning storm that feeds on warm sea water. India has seas on both sides, but the Bay of Bengal, to the east, produces far more cyclones than the Arabian Sea to the west. Over the past century, the ratio has been roughly four to one.

Several things make the Bay a better cyclone factory. Its surface water is usually warmer. Rivers like [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]] and Brahmaputra pour in huge amounts of fresh water, which floats on top and keeps the warm layer from mixing with cold water below. And the Bay receives leftover storms that drift in from the Pacific Ocean.
The shape of the coast makes things worse. The Bay narrows towards Bangladesh and West Bengal, and its shallow edges can pile sea water into a dangerous wall called a storm surge.

st.prompt: In 1999, a super cyclone in Odisha killed around 10,000 people. In 2013, Cyclone Phailin was almost as strong. What happened?

options.t: Far fewer people died, because of early warnings and mass evacuation

st.reveal: Phailin made landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha. Forecasters tracked it for days, and around a million people were moved to shelters. Fewer than 50 people are thought to have died, a fraction of the 1999 toll.

sec.t:
[[@hurricanes|Cyclones and hurricanes]] are the same kind of storm with different names. They start over warm sea water, usually above about 26 °C. Warm, moist air rises, cools and forms towering clouds. As the water vapour turns to rain, it releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster.

Air rushes in at the bottom to replace it. Because the Earth spins, that incoming air starts to turn. In the Northern Hemisphere it [[@maths-golden-spiral|spirals anticlockwise]]. When the winds reach about 62 km/h, the [[@imd|India Meteorological Department]] calls the system a cyclonic storm and gives it a name.

The Arabian Sea is cooler for several reasons. Strong winds near Somalia and Oman stir up cold water from the deep. Dry, dusty air blows off the deserts of Arabia. Both make storms harder to grow.

The Bay of Bengal is different. A thin layer of fresh river water sits on top of the salty sea. It traps warmth near the surface, so a passing storm finds a deep supply of heat to feed on. The Bay also gets help from the east. Typhoons from the South China Sea sometimes cross Myanmar or Thailand, weaken over land, then strengthen again once they reach the warm water.

India's cyclone seasons come either side of the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]: April to May, and October to December.

{{story:mangroves}}

The Bay has seen terrible storms. In 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck what is now Bangladesh and killed hundreds of thousands of people. In 1999, a super cyclone hit Odisha, killing about 10,000.

After that, [[@odisha|Odisha]] built hundreds of cyclone shelters and trained volunteers in villages. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] and better computer models made [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] far more accurate. When Cyclone Phailin arrived in 2013, around a million people were moved to safety. Fewer than 50 are thought to have died. In 2019, the state did it again for Cyclone Fani.

Nature helps too. Thick [[@mangroves|mangrove]] forests, like the Sundarbans, slow down storm surges and protect villages behind them.

sec.h: Is the Arabian Sea catching up?
sec.t:
In recent years, the Arabian Sea has produced some strong cyclones, such as Tauktae in 2021 and Biparjoy in 2023. Its surface waters have been warming, and several studies have found that strong cyclones there have become more frequent. Scientists are still working out how much of this is part of a long-term trend and how much is natural variation.

The names come from a list agreed by 13 countries around the region, including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Oman. Each country suggests names, and they are used in turn.

text: The water in your tap comes from rivers, lakes, [[reservoir|reservoirs]] or underground, and before that it fell as rain or snow. It is part of the water cycle: the Sun warms seas, lakes and plants, water [[evaporation|evaporates]] into the air, cools into clouds, and falls again as rain. Then it flows back towards the sea, and the cycle starts again.

Your local water company collects some of that water on its way, cleans it, and pipes it to your home. After you use it, it goes down the drain, is cleaned again, and returns to rivers and the sea. Not one drop is new.

st.prompt: After water evaporates from the sea, how long does it stay in the air, on average, before falling as rain or snow?
st.reveal: The US Geological Survey estimates that water stays in the atmosphere for about nine days on average. Water in the deep ocean or an ice sheet, by contrast, can stay put for thousands of years.

Water evaporates, condenses on the cold film like a cloud, and drips into the cup like rain.
myth: The world is running out of water because we use it up.

The total amount of water on Earth stays almost the same, moving around the water cycle. What can run short is clean fresh water in the right place at the right time, which is why droughts and pollution matter so much.

sec.t:
The Sun drives the water cycle. It heats the oceans, and water rises into the air as invisible vapour. Plants add more, giving off water through tiny holes in their leaves. High up, the air is colder, and the vapour cools into tiny droplets around specks of dust. Millions of droplets together make a cloud.

When the droplets join up and get heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow. Some soaks into the ground. Some runs off into streams and rivers. Some freezes into [[glacier|glaciers]] and stays there for centuries. Sooner or later, almost all of it makes its way back to the sea.

Earth has a lot of water, but about 97.5% of it is salty seawater. Most of the fresh water is locked up in [[@what-if-ice-melted|ice sheets]] and [[@glaciers|glaciers]] or hidden deep underground. The fresh water in lakes, rivers and swamps is well under 1% of all the water on Earth.

That small share supplies most of the world's farms, factories and homes. So where your tap water comes from depends a great deal on where you live.

sec.h: From the river to your tap

sec.t:
Not all tap water comes from rivers. Much of it comes from groundwater, water that has soaked into the soil and collected in cracks and spaces in rock. People reach it with wells and borewells.

India uses more groundwater than any other country. Farmers pump it to water their fields, and many towns depend on it. In some places, wells are being emptied faster than rain can refill them, and the water table is dropping. Rainwater harvesting, catching rain on roofs and guiding it into the ground, is one way people are trying to help.

River and lake water carries mud, leaves and germs, so it is [[@water-purify|cleaned]] before it reaches you. At a water treatment plant, the water is left to settle so mud sinks. Then it is filtered through sand and gravel, and disinfected, usually with a small amount of chlorine, to kill germs.

After you use water, it goes down the drain into [[@toilets-sewers|sewers]]. In many cities, it is cleaned at a sewage treatment plant before being released into a river. Downstream, another town might take it in, clean it again, and pipe it to someone else's tap.

The water cycle has been turning for billions of years. The same water has fallen as rain, flowed down rivers and frozen into ice again and again. Some of the water in your glass may once have been in a cloud over the Himalaya, a lake in Africa or a glacier in the last Ice Age.

text: Yes. The oldest shark-like scales ever found are about 450 million years old. The first trees appeared around 385 million years ago. So sharks were cruising the seas for tens of millions of years before any forest grew on land.

Sharks are also much older than dinosaurs, which appeared about 230 million years ago. Since then, sharks have lived through [[@dino-extinction-theories|several mass extinctions]], including the one that [[@what-if-dinos-lived|wiped out the dinosaurs]], as you can read in [[@who-survived|who survived]].
The sharks of long ago didn't look exactly like today's. But the basic plan, a fast, streamlined hunter with a skeleton of rubbery [[cartilage|cartilage]], has lasted an astonishingly long time.

st.prompt: Which came first?
st.reveal: Sharks! The oldest shark scales are about 450 million years old. The first trees appeared around 385 million years ago. Dinosaurs came much later, about 230 million years ago.
st.nudge: Trees seem so ancient! But sharks beat them by tens of millions of years.

myth: All sharks must keep swimming or they will die.

Some sharks, like the great white, do need to keep moving so water flows over their gills. But many others, such as nurse sharks, can rest on the seabed and pump water over their gills while lying still.

sec.t:
Shark skeletons are made of cartilage, the same bendy stuff as the tip of your nose. Cartilage rots away quickly, so whole [[fossil|fossil]] sharks are rare. Instead, scientists mostly find teeth and tiny scales, which are hard like bone.

Luckily, sharks shed teeth all their lives. A shark has rows of spare teeth lined up behind the front ones, moving forward like a conveyor belt. One shark can lose thousands in its lifetime. Compare that with your own [[@teeth|teeth]]: just two sets. Beaches near Venice, Florida, are so full of fossil shark teeth that people sift the sand for them.

Sharks can [[@nose-smell|smell]] blood in the water from a long way off. A line of [[sensor|sensors]] along each side of the body feels the tiniest ripples. And tiny jelly-filled pores on a shark's snout can pick up the faint electric signals made by the muscles of a hiding fish.

Some sharks live astonishingly long. In 2016, scientists studied [[@extreme-longest-living|Greenland sharks]] and estimated that one was nearly 400 years old, give or take more than a century. Even the low end of that guess makes it the longest-living animal with a backbone known.

Today's biggest fish is the whale shark, which can grow longer than a city bus. Despite its size, it eats only tiny [[plankton|plankton]] and small fish. Every year, whale sharks visit the coast of Gujarat.

Fishermen there once hunted them. In 2001, India made the whale shark the first fish protected under its wildlife law. Campaigners worked with local leaders, including the spiritual teacher Morari Bapu, who compared the whale shark to a daughter coming home to her parents. Now many fishermen cut their own nets to free a trapped whale shark.

[[@sharks-myths|Sharks bite fewer than a hundred people]] worldwide in a typical year. The 1975 [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] film *Jaws* made audiences around the world afraid of them anyway, and the novel's author, Peter Benchley, later campaigned to protect sharks. People, meanwhile, catch many millions of sharks every year. Many are caught by accident in nets meant for other fish, and some are killed only for their fins. Today about a third of all kinds of sharks and rays are threatened.

That is a strange twist. Sharks were already ancient when the first trees took root, long before giants like the [[@redwoods|redwoods]] appeared. After 450 million years, the biggest danger they have ever faced may be us.

text: Throw a ball up and [[gravity|gravity]] drags it back. Throw it harder and it goes higher before falling. Escape [[velocity|velocity]] is the speed that is just enough to never fall back, because gravity can slow the ball down but never quite stop it.

For Earth, that speed is about 11.2 km per second, or roughly 40,000 km/h. At that pace you could cross from Mumbai to Delhi in under two minutes. A bullet from a rifle travels only about a tenth as fast.

But here is the twist. Escape velocity is for something thrown once and left to coast, like a cannonball. A rocket keeps firing its engines, so in theory it could climb away slowly. In practice, slow climbing wastes fuel fighting gravity, so rockets go fast anyway.

st.prompt: Which would need a higher speed to escape from Earth's surface, a cricket ball or a fully loaded truck?

options.t: The truck, because it is heavier
The cricket ball, because it is lighter

st.reveal: Escape velocity depends only on the planet's mass and size, not on what you throw. The truck needs much more energy to reach that speed, but the speed itself is the same, about 11.2 km per second.

d.try: Throw a soft ball straight up gently, then harder, and count how many seconds it takes to come down each time. Every extra bit of speed buys more time in the air. Escape velocity is the speed at which the ball would never come back at all.
myth: Once a rocket gets high enough, there is no gravity in space.

Gravity reaches out forever, getting weaker with distance. Astronauts on the space station feel weightless because they are falling around Earth all the time, while gravity there is still about 90 per cent as strong as on the ground.
facts: Speed to stay in low orbit
more than the speed of light

sec.t:
More than 300 years ago, Isaac Newton drew a famous picture. It showed a cannon on top of a very tall mountain, firing balls sideways. A slow ball curves down and lands nearby. A faster one lands farther away. Fire one fast enough, and the ground curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. The ball never lands. It is in [[orbit|orbit]].

For low orbit around Earth, that speed is about 7.8 km per second. Push faster still, to 11.2 km per second, and the orbit stretches into a path that never comes back. That is escape.

sec.h: Why heavy and light need the same speed
Why not just fire a cannon?
sec.t:
In 1865, the French writer Jules Verne wrote about launching people to the Moon from a giant cannon in Florida. It makes a great story but terrible science. The air near the ground is thick. Anything moving at 11 km per second would heat up like a [[meteor|meteor]] and burn. And the sudden push would crush any passengers.

That's why rockets start slowly, climb out of the thick air first, and then speed up. They burn fuel for several minutes, gaining speed bit by bit.

sec.h: India's clever way to the Moon
sec.t:
[[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]], which landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023, did not blast straight off at escape speed. Its rocket put it in a long oval orbit around Earth. Then the spacecraft fired its own small engine several times at the closest point of each loop, stretching the orbit bigger and bigger, like a child pumping higher on a swing.

Finally, one last burn flung it towards the Moon. The trip took about 40 days instead of three, but it saved a lot of fuel. Small, carefully timed pushes added up to the speed it needed.

Some objects have escape velocities that are almost beyond belief. To leave the surface of the Sun, you would need about 618 km per second. And for a [[@black-holes|black hole]], the escape velocity is faster than light itself, about 300,000 km per second. Since nothing can go that fast, nothing that falls in ever gets out. Not even the light, which is why it looks black.

text: Beethoven composed when he was deaf by hearing the music in his mind. By the time his hearing failed, he had spent more than twenty years playing, studying and writing music. He knew exactly how each note and each instrument would sound, the way you can "hear" a familiar song in your head without any sound at all.

He worked out his ideas in sketchbooks, writing and rewriting themes until they were right. Some of his greatest works, including the Ninth Symphony, were written when he could hardly hear anything. He could not hear them played, but he knew how they would sound.

st.prompt: When his Ninth Symphony was first performed in 1824, how much could Beethoven hear?
st.reveal: He was almost completely deaf by then. People who were there later said that at the end, someone had to turn him round so he could see the audience cheering.

sec.t:
Ludwig van Beethoven was born in December 1770 in Bonn, in today's [[@germany|Germany]]. His father, a singer, pushed him hard, hoping he would become a child star like [[@mozart|Mozart]].

In 1792, Beethoven moved to Vienna, the music capital of Europe, and studied for a while with the composer Joseph Haydn. He became famous as a dazzling pianist who could make up music on the spot. Rich music lovers paid him to compose. His music was often bold and stormy, and it pushed the [[@piano|pianos]] of the day to their limits.

For a time, Beethoven used ear trumpets, metal horns held to the ear to gather sound. As his hearing got worse, they stopped helping.

From 1818, friends and visitors talked to him by writing in notebooks, and he answered aloud. About 140 of these conversation books survive. They show him chatting about music, money, food and his nephew. A story says he also sawed the legs off a piano so he could feel its [[vibration|vibrations]] through the floor, but historians are unsure how true some of these tales are. Sound can travel through solid materials, as explained in [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]].

On 7 May 1824, Beethoven's Ninth Symphony was first performed in Vienna. For the last part, he did something new: he added singers and [[@choirs|a choir]] to a symphony, singing a poem about joy and friendship.

Beethoven stood on stage beside the conductor, beating time. People who were there later said that when the music ended, he was still facing the orchestra. One of the singers turned him round to see the crowd clapping and waving their hats.

The melody from that last part, known as "Ode to Joy", is now the anthem of the European Union. His Fifth Symphony starts with four famous notes, "da-da-da-DUM", which may be the best-known opening in classical music.

Beethoven died in Vienna in 1827. Thousands of people are said to have followed his funeral procession. His life is often held up as a story of courage. It is also a story about how much of music happens in the mind, where he kept hearing it long after his ears had stopped.

text: When a song gives you chills, your brain is doing two things at once. It is predicting what comes next, and it is rewarding you when the music delivers.

Brain scans show that the brain releases [[dopamine|dopamine]], a chemical linked to pleasure and wanting, both while you wait for a favourite moment and when it arrives. That rush can set off the same reflex that makes your skin prickle in the cold. Tiny [[@muscles|muscles]] at the base of each hair tighten, and the hairs stand up.
Not everyone gets [[@body-music-chills|music chills]]. Many people do, and some never have. Scientists are still finding out why.

st.prompt: What do you think causes musical goosebumps?

options.t: Your brain enjoys what it expected

st.reveal: It's your brain! When music builds up, your brain guesses what's coming. When the big moment arrives, it releases dopamine, a feel-good chemical, and that can trigger shivers.
st.nudge: Goosebumps do happen when we're cold! But with music, it's your brain at work.

src: Salimpoor V.N. et al. (2011) Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music. Nature Neuroscience 14.
Sachs M.E. et al. (2016) Brain connectivity reflects human aesthetic responses to music. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 11.
n.certNote: The dopamine finding is well studied. Why only some people get chills, and why music borrows an old body reflex, is still being researched.

d.try: Make a chills chart with a friend or family member. Each of you picks three songs you love. Listen together, and raise a hand whenever you feel a shiver or a tingle. Write down the exact moment in each song. Do your moments match, or does the same song move each of you in a different place?
myth: Goosebumps only happen when you're cold.
Cold is one trigger, but fear, surprise and strong emotion can set off the same reflex. For many people, a powerful moment in music is enough.

sec.t:
Scientists call these musical chills "frisson", a French word for a shiver. In a well-known study published in 2011, researchers at McGill University in Montreal asked people to bring their own favourite pieces of music. Then they played the music while scanning the listeners' brains.

They found dopamine released in two different places. One area became active in the seconds before a chill, as the listener sensed a big moment coming. Another became active at the peak itself. In other words, the waiting was part of the pleasure. The same reward system in the [[@brain-works|brain]] helps us enjoy food and other treats, which may be why a great song can feel almost delicious.

sec.h: Why some people and not others
sec.t:
Researchers have found that people who often get chills tend to score high on a personality trait called "openness to experience". They enjoy new ideas, art and daydreaming. A small brain-scan study in 2016 suggested that people who get chills may have stronger connections between the parts of the brain that process sound and those that handle feelings.

Culture and memory matter too. A song tied to a wedding, a festival or a [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] night can move you more than a song you hear for the first time. So the same piece might give one person goosebumps and leave the friend beside them yawning.

Goosebumps are left over from our furry ancestors. When a cat is frightened, its fur puffs up to make it look bigger. When a bird is cold, it fluffs its feathers to trap warm air. Humans have too little hair for either trick to work, but the reflex survived.

Why music should borrow it is still debated. One idea is that powerful music stirs ancient alarm and reward systems in the brain, the ones that once reacted to danger or to a parent's call. Whatever the reason, [[@sound-travel|sound waves]] arriving at your ears can make the skin on your arms react. That is a long way for a tremble in the air to travel.

text: Yakshagana is a traditional theatre from coastal [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] that mixes dance, music, singing and spoken dialogue. Its name means "songs of the yakshas", magical beings from Hindu stories. Performances tell tales from the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], the Ramayana and the Puranas, with gods, kings, heroes and demons.

Actors wear bright costumes, large wooden ornaments and towering, decorated crowns. A singer called the Bhagavata leads the show from the back of the stage, singing the story while drummers pound out the [[rhythm|rhythm]]. The actors dance to the songs, then step forward and speak, making up much of their dialogue on the spot. Traditionally, shows run all night in the open air, ending at sunrise.

options.t: The Bhagavata, a singer sitting with the musicians
A narrator who walks among the audience

st.reveal: The Bhagavata sits at the back of the stage with the drummers. He sings the verses, keeps time with small cymbals and directs the actors, who then act out and expand each verse with dance and dialogue.

d.try: Play "Bhagavata" with friends. One person sings or reads a single line of a story out loud, such as "The king enters, angry". The actor then has to make up what the king says and does, with no script. Swap roles and see how differently each person tells the same line.
myth: Yakshagana is a kind of Kathakali.

They are separate traditions from neighbouring states. Both use big costumes and stories from the epics, but Yakshagana actors speak and improvise dialogue in Kannada, while Kathakali actors never speak.

sec.t:
The Bhagavata is the heart of Yakshagana. He sits on a low platform with the musicians and sings the verses of the play. He also keeps the beat with small cymbals and signals the actors when to move, when to speak and when to stop.

Beside him sit the drummers. The *chande* is a tall drum played with sticks, loud enough to be heard across the fields at night. The *maddale* is a two-sided drum played with the hands, giving softer, deeper sounds. A [[@harmonium|harmonium]] or a drone instrument holds the main note.

The costumes are among the most striking in [[@indian-theatre|Indian theatre]]. Kings and heroes wear a tall crown called a *kireeta*. Demons and fierce characters wear the huge *kedage mundale*, a fan-shaped headdress that can be wider than the actor's shoulders.

Ornaments are carved from light wood, covered with gold foil and set with small pieces of mirror and coloured glass. Faces are painted in bold colours, with patterns that show each character's nature. Fully dressed, an actor looks almost twice their normal size, which makes sense for a show watched by crowds sitting on the ground in the dark.

Yakshagana troupes are called *melas*, and many are linked to temples. From about November to May, the dry season after the [[monsoon|monsoon]], they travel from village to village, setting up a stage and lights in open fields. Families sponsor shows to give thanks or to fulfil a vow.

Thousands of people may come, bringing mats to sit on. Children fall asleep and wake up to see a demon in full fury at 3 a.m. There are two main styles: Tenkutittu in the south, closer to Kerala, and Badagutittu in the north, around Udupi.

Yakshagana also has a seated form called *talamaddale*. The actors sit in a row in everyday clothes, and the Bhagavata sings as usual. There is no dancing at all. Instead, the performers debate the story in long, clever arguments, almost like a courtroom.

In the 20th century, the writer K. Shivarama Karanth experimented with Yakshagana, shortening shows and taking troupes abroad. Today it is also performed in Tulu, the other major language of the coast. Its mix of music, dance and improvised [[@theatre|theatre]] still draws large crowds.

text: Young people have changed the world many times, usually by joining together and refusing to accept something they thought was wrong. They have marched, gone on strike from school, written, spoken in public and simply showed up where they weren't wanted.

Some became famous, like Malala Yousafzai, who spoke up for girls' education, or Greta Thunberg, who started a school strike for the [[climate|climate]] at 15. Many more are unknown: the thousands of students who left their colleges during India's freedom struggle, or the children who marched for civil rights in the US. Change usually came from crowds, not lone heroes.

sec.t:
On 14 November 1960, Ruby Bridges, aged six, became the first Black child to attend William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans. Crowds shouted at her. Four US marshals walked her in. Most white parents pulled their children out, and for most of that year she was taught alone by one teacher, Barbara Henry.

In 1963, in Birmingham, Alabama, civil rights leaders asked children and teenagers to march, because many adults feared losing their jobs. Over several days in May, more than a thousand young people were arrested. The protests became a turning point in the [[@civil-rights|civil rights movement]].

In Pakistan's Swat Valley, an armed group banned girls from going to school. A schoolgirl named Malala Yousafzai wrote a blog about it, and spoke on TV. In 2012, when she was 15, a gunman attacked her on her school bus. She survived, recovered in Britain and kept campaigning.

In 2014 she shared the Nobel Peace Prize with [[@kailash-satyarthi|Kailash Satyarthi]], an Indian activist who has spent decades rescuing children from forced labour. At 17, she was the youngest person ever to win it.

In August 2018, Greta Thunberg, a 15-year-old in Sweden, began sitting outside her country's [[parliament|parliament]] with a hand-painted sign reading "School strike for climate". Other students joined. By September 2019, millions of people in many countries had taken part in climate strikes.

Young people in India have joined too, protesting about air pollution in Delhi and the cutting of trees in cities like Mumbai and Bengaluru. Not everyone agrees with school strikes. Some adults say students should stay in class. Others say young people have the most at stake, because they will live with climate change the longest. Many have moved on from strikes to quieter work on [[@climate-action|climate action]], such as planting trees or pushing their schools to use solar power.

Movements led by young people often share a few things. Young people may have less to lose, like jobs or businesses, and more time to organise. They are often quick to use new tools, from printed pamphlets in the 1920s to social media today.

They also ask simple, hard questions. Why can't she come to our school? Why are we still burning coal? A question like that is easy to understand and hard to wave away. It's one reason the UN's Convention on the [[@rights-kids|Rights of the Child]], agreed in 1989, says children have a right to be heard on matters that affect them.

text: Mango prices change because of two forces economists call supply and demand. Supply is how many mangoes are for sale. Demand is how many people want them and can pay for them.

Early in the season, in March, only a few mangoes have ripened, but people are desperate for the first taste of summer. Few mangoes plus lots of eager buyers means high prices. By May the trees are loaded and markets overflow with fruit. Now sellers have more mangoes than buyers want, so they cut prices to sell them before they rot. The mango is the same. The balance between sellers and buyers is not.

st.prompt: A hailstorm destroys half of a region's mango crop just before harvest. People want mangoes as much as ever. What happens to the price?
st.reveal: With fewer mangoes for sale and the same number of hungry buyers, sellers can ask more. Some buyers drop out, and the price settles where the smaller supply matches the people still willing to pay.

sec.t:
You can think of a price as a seesaw. On one end sit the sellers, on the other the buyers. If something is scarce, buyers compete for it and the price rises. If there is too much, sellers compete for customers and the price falls.

Prices also send messages. A high price tells farmers that people want more, so it is worth growing. A low price tells them to try something else. That is how millions of strangers, who never meet, end up roughly matching what is grown with what is eaten. Studying this is one of the first things you learn in [[@economics-kids|economics]].

sec.h: When the weather sets the price
sec.t:
Farming depends on the weather, so food prices jump with it. In late 2019, heavy rains damaged onion crops in western India, and in some cities onion prices climbed past ₹100 a kilo. Families noticed it in every curry.

The USA had a similar shock in early 2025, when bird flu killed millions of egg-laying hens. With far fewer eggs for sale, prices hit a record. Shops limited how many cartons each customer could buy. A [[@farm-to-plate|farm-to-plate]] chain is long, so a problem at the start shows up at the end.

Some prices are not left entirely to the market. The Indian government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a minimum support price, so a bumper harvest doesn't ruin them. It also sells grain cheaply to poorer families through ration shops. These rules soften the seesaw, though economists argue about how well they work and what they cost.

{{story:farm-to-plate}}

Supply and demand work almost everywhere. Train and plane tickets cost more at Diwali or Thanksgiving, when everyone wants to travel home at once. Ride-hailing apps raise prices when it rains and few cabs are free. Shops use the same idea in reverse. Winter jackets go on sale at the end of winter, because a shop would rather sell them cheaply than store them for a year. A ticket to a World Cup final costs far more than a ticket to a practice match in the same stadium.

Sometimes demand jumps suddenly. During the early weeks of the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]] in 2020, masks and hand sanitiser sold out in [[@shops-markets|shops]] across the world and prices shot up until factories caught up.

People have found ways to even out the swings. Cold storage lets farmers keep potatoes and apples for months and sell them later. Mangoes are harder, because they spoil quickly, so families turn the glut into pickles, aam papad and pulp. Shops also bring fruit from other regions or countries where the season falls at a different time.

Different [[@mango-varieties|mango varieties]] ripen at different times too. Alphonso and Kesar come early, Langra and Dasheri a little later, and some kinds hold on into July. If you want cheap mangoes, wait for the middle of the season. If you want the first one of the year, be ready to pay for it.

text: Morse code turns letters and numbers into patterns of short and long signals, called dots and dashes. A dot is a quick signal. A dash lasts three times as long. The letter A is dot-dash. B is dash-dot-dot-dot. SOS is dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot.

The signals can be anything that can be switched on and off: electric pulses along a wire, beeps on a radio, flashes of light or taps on a pipe. Gaps matter too. A short gap separates the parts of a letter, a longer gap separates letters and a longer one still separates words.
With just two signals, Morse code can spell any message, a bit like the [[@number-zero-one|0s and 1s]] of [[@binary-code|binary code]] that computers use today.

st.reveal: Common letters got short codes so messages could be sent faster. E is the most common letter in English, so it got one dot. T, the second most common, got one dash. Rare letters like Q and Z got longer codes.

SOS doesn't stand for anything. It was chosen because the pattern of three dots, three dashes and three dots is simple, quick and hard to confuse with anything else. The phrases came later as ways to remember it.

sec.t:
Samuel Morse was an American painter. In 1825, while he was away painting a portrait, his wife became ill and died. The letter telling him took days to arrive, and he got home too late. Some historians think this helped spark his interest in faster ways to send news.

In the 1830s, Morse worked on an electric [[@telegraph|telegraph]] that sent pulses of electricity along a wire. With his partner Alfred Vail, he developed a code to go with it. On 24 May 1844, Morse sent a message on a new line from Washington to Baltimore. It was a line from the Bible: "What hath God wrought".

Within a few decades, [[telegraph|telegraph]] wires crossed continents, and [[@undersea-internet|cables under the oceans]] linked them.

Morse and Vail made a smart choice. Letters used often got short codes, and rare letters got long ones. E, the most common letter in English, is a single dot. T is a single dash. Q is dash-dash-dot-dash.

It is said that Vail worked out which letters were most common by counting the metal letters in a printer's type box. The more pieces of type a printer kept for a letter, the more often it was used.

This idea of giving common things short codes is still used in computers today, to squeeze files into less space.

{{story:titanic}}

Ships at sea used [[@radio-waves|radio]] Morse code from the early 1900s. They needed a distress call that anyone would recognise. In 1906, an international meeting in Berlin chose SOS, and it came into use in 1908.

On the night of 15 April 1912, the radio operators on the sinking [[@titanic|Titanic]] sent both the older call, CQD, and the newer SOS. Ships that heard them raced to help, and one, the *Carpathia*, rescued the survivors from the lifeboats.

India's first experimental telegraph line opened in 1851 between Calcutta, now Kolkata, and Diamond Harbour, about 50 km away. Within a few years, lines linked Calcutta, Agra, Bombay, Madras and Peshawar. Telegrams carried news of births, deaths, exam results and jobs for generations.

As mobile phones and [[@email|email]] took over, fewer people sent telegrams. India's state telegraph service sent its last messages on 14 July 2013, after 162 years. People queued at telegraph offices to send one final telegram as a keepsake.

Morse code is no longer used by big ships, which switched to satellite systems in 1999. But amateur radio operators around the world still send and receive it for fun.

Pilots also hear it. Radio beacons near airports send their short identity codes in Morse, so pilots can check they are tuned to the right one. And because it needs only a switch, Morse has helped some people with disabilities communicate by [[@blinking|blinking]] or tapping.

text: American football is a game of two teams of 11 players on a long field. One team attacks, called the offense, and tries to carry or throw an oval ball into the other team's end zone. The other team, the defense, tries to stop them by tackling whoever has the ball.

The attackers get four tries, called downs, to move the ball forward 10 yards. If they manage it, they get four more tries. If they fail, the other team takes over. Touchdowns score six points. Kicking the ball between the tall goalposts scores three.

st.reveal: If the team moves the ball 10 yards within four downs, it gets a fresh set of four. If not, the other team takes over. That simple rule is the heartbeat of the whole game.

sec.t:
Unlike [[@football-world|soccer]], American football stops and starts. Each play, called a down, lasts only a few seconds. The teams line up facing each other at the line of scrimmage, the ball is passed back to the quarterback, and then everyone explodes into action.

The quarterback might hand the ball to a runner, or throw it far downfield to a receiver. When the ball carrier is tackled or runs out of bounds, the play ends. The teams huddle, plan the next move and line up again. The playing time is four 15-minute quarters, but stoppages mean a game usually lasts around three hours.

The game grew out of rugby and soccer, which were both played at American colleges in the 1800s. The first college game, between Rutgers and Princeton in 1869, looked more like soccer. A Yale player and coach called Walter Camp then changed the rules in the 1880s, adding the line of scrimmage and the system of downs. He is often called the father of American football.

Early games were brutal, and players died. In 1905 President Theodore Roosevelt called college leaders to the [[@white-house|White House]] to make the game safer. The forward pass was allowed the next year, which spread players out and changed the game for ever.

sec.h: The NFL and the Super Bowl
sec.t:
The National Football League was founded in 1920 in Canton, Ohio. Its championship game, the [[@super-bowl|Super Bowl]], was first played in January 1967. It is now usually the most watched [[@television-invented|television]] broadcast in the United States each year, and companies pay millions for a 30-second advert.

Many Americans care just as much about high school and college football. In [[@texas|Texas]], some high school stadiums hold more than 15,000 fans on a Friday night.

American football is a collision sport, and players wear [[@helmets|helmets]] and pads. Doctors have found that repeated blows to the head can cause long-term brain damage, even without a serious single injury. Since about 2010 the NFL has changed rules to reduce head-to-head hits and protect players.

[[@sports-science|Sports scientists]] are designing better helmets, and many youth leagues now play flag football. Instead of tackling, players pull a flag from the ball carrier's belt. It keeps the plays and the strategy while dropping the hardest hits, a little like a game of [[@kabaddi|kabaddi]] without the wrestling.

text: Jeans began in 1873 as hard-wearing work trousers in the American West. A tailor named Jacob Davis put small copper rivets at the corners of the pockets so they would not tear. He teamed up with Levi Strauss, a cloth seller in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]], and the two got a patent.

Miners, farmers, cowboys and railway workers wore them for decades. Then, in the 1950s, film stars and teenagers made jeans a symbol of youth and rebellion. From there they spread around the world, and today they are worn by almost everyone, from schoolchildren to grandparents.

sec.h: A tailor, a merchant and some rivets
sec.t:
Jacob Davis was a tailor in Reno, Nevada. Around 1870, a customer asked for trousers that would not fall apart. Davis hammered copper rivets at the weak points, where pockets usually ripped. The trousers sold well, but Davis could not afford a patent.

He wrote to Levi Strauss, who supplied his cloth. Strauss paid, and on 20 May 1873 the two received a US patent for riveted work trousers. Davis moved to San Francisco to run the factory. Their trousers were first called "waist overalls", not jeans.

The blue comes from indigo, one of the oldest dyes in the world. For centuries much of it came from the indigo plant grown in India, and the word itself comes from the Greek for "Indian". Under British rule, many farmers in Bengal and Bihar were forced to grow indigo instead of food.

In 1917, Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] went to Champaran in Bihar to investigate the indigo farmers' complaints. It was his first major campaign in India. By then, German chemists had found a way to make indigo in factories, and from 1897 [[@accident-mauve|synthetic indigo]] began replacing the plant.

Indigo does not soak right into cotton. It clings to the outside of each thread. That's why jeans fade with washing and wear, showing white at the knees and pockets.

In the 1930s, holidaymakers from American cities visited ranches in the West and brought jeans home. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], American soldiers wore them off duty and carried them abroad.

Then came the 1950s. Young film stars wore jeans in films about rebellious teenagers, and some schools in the USA banned them. That made them even more popular with the young. By the 1970s, jeans were sold everywhere, in every shape: flared, straight, tight and baggy.

Making one pair of jeans uses a lot of water, mostly to grow the cotton. Estimates run into thousands of litres for a single pair, depending on where the cotton is grown and how it is watered. Dyeing and washing add more.

Some companies now recycle old jeans, use less water when finishing them and grow cotton more carefully. Wearing jeans longer, washing them less often and passing them on all help too. Many people already do this without thinking, because old jeans are usually the most comfortable kind.

sec.t:
In the 1850s, a French printer named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville built a machine he called the phonautograph. Sound made a thin sheet vibrate, and a bristle attached to it traced wavy lines onto paper blackened with soot. He wanted to study the shapes of sounds, not hear them again.

In 2008, scientists in the USA scanned one of his papers from 1860 and turned the lines back into sound using a computer. Out came a faint voice singing a French folk song, "Au clair de la lune". It is the oldest known recording of a human voice.

In 1902, the Gramophone Company sent [[@behind-music-recording|recording engineers]] to [[@kolkata|Calcutta]]. There they recorded Gauhar Jaan, a famous singer and dancer. She was one of the first Indian singers recorded on a gramophone disc, and became India's first recording star. She went on to record hundreds of songs in more than ten languages.

Each side of a disc held only about three minutes, so singers squeezed long [[raga|ragas]] into short versions. At the end of each recording, Gauhar Jaan announced, "My name is Gauhar Jaan", so the engineers could label the discs.

Early recordings were made without [[@electricity-made|electricity]]: performers crowded around a big horn. From the 1920s, [[@microphones|microphones]] turned sound into electrical signals, giving much clearer recordings. During the 1930s and 1940s, magnetic tape arrived, letting engineers cut and join recordings.

In 1948, long-playing vinyl records held over 20 minutes a side. Bands like the [[@beatles-india|Beatles]] sold millions. In 1963, Philips introduced the compact cassette. Cheap cassette players and recorders arrived in India in the 1980s, and companies such as T-Series sold [[@film-songs|film songs]] and devotional music at low prices. Music shops opened in towns that had never had a record shop.

In 1982, compact discs went on sale. Inside a CD, sound is measured 44,100 times every second, and each measurement is stored as a number in [[@binary-code|binary]]. A laser reads the numbers, and a chip turns them back into sound.

Then came MP3 files, which shrank music by throwing away sounds most ears do not notice. Today, [[@streaming|streaming]] services send those numbers to your phone over the internet in a moment. A song that once needed a needle, a horn and a turning disc now fits in your pocket, along with millions of others.

text: When you run, your leg muscles suddenly need much more oxygen and fuel, and they produce more waste, such as [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. [[@blood|Blood]] carries oxygen to muscles and takes the waste away. So the faster the muscles work, the faster blood has to flow.

Your heart does two things to keep up. It beats more often, and it squeezes harder, pushing out more blood with each beat. At the same time you breathe faster and deeper, so [[@lungs-breathe|your lungs]] can load more oxygen into that blood.
None of this needs you to think. Your brain and body handle it automatically.

st.prompt: Top endurance athletes often have a resting heart rate that is...
st.reveal: Training makes the heart stronger, so it pushes out more blood with every beat. At rest it doesn't need to beat as often. Some long-distance runners and cyclists rest at around 40 beats a minute or even lower.

sec.t:
At rest, an adult's heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute, roughly a bucketful. During hard [[@exercise|exercise]], a fit adult's heart can pump 20 litres or more. Children's hearts are smaller and beat faster, but they speed up in the same way.

Your heart also has a top speed. A rough rule of thumb says your maximum heart rate is about 220 minus your age, so around 208 beats a minute for a 12-year-old. It's only a guide, since people differ a lot, but it shows how much room for speeding up a young heart has.

It is a bit like a cricket team in the final overs of a chase. The batters run harder between wickets and hit bigger shots at the same time, because the target is getting closer.

Pumping blood out is only half the job. It also has to come back up from your feet, against [[gravity|gravity]]. Here your leg [[@muscles|muscles]] help. Each time they squeeze, they press on [[vein|veins]], which have little one-way valves inside, and push blood back towards the heart.

This is why soldiers standing still for a long time sometimes faint, while people walking around rarely do. Moving muscles act like a second pump.

Your heart is a muscle, and like other muscles it gets stronger with regular exercise. A trained heart pumps more blood per beat, so it can beat more slowly at rest.

Elite [[@running-marathon|marathon runners]] and cyclists often have resting heart rates of 40 or even lower. Doctors generally say a normal adult resting rate is about 60 to 100 beats a minute. Children's rates are higher, and babies' are higher still.

When you stop running, your heart doesn't drop straight back to normal. It slows over a few minutes as your muscles clear out their waste and your breathing settles. The quicker it recovers, the fitter you usually are.

Over a lifetime, a human heart beats around two and a half to three billion times. A mouse's heart can beat over 500 times a minute, while a diving [[@blue-whale|blue whale]]'s can slow to just two or three beats a minute.

text: Rubber comes from latex, a milky sap that oozes from cuts in the bark of rubber trees. On its own, dried latex is a poor material. It turns sticky and smelly in hot weather and stiff and brittle in cold.

In 1839, an American inventor named Charles Goodyear heated rubber mixed with sulphur. The rubber stopped melting and stopped cracking. The process came to be called vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. Almost every rubber thing you touch, from [[@tyres|tyres]] to shoe soles, is made this way.

st.prompt: What did Charles Goodyear mix with rubber and heat to make it tough and springy?
st.reveal: Heated with sulphur, rubber's long chain molecules get tied together by tiny sulphur bridges. The rubber stops melting in heat and stays bendy in cold.

d.try: Put one rubber band in the freezer for an hour and keep another at room temperature. Stretch both and compare. Then stretch a band quickly and touch it gently to your forehead. You may feel it warm up as its chain molecules line up.
myth: Charles Goodyear started the Goodyear tyre company.
He died in 1860, deeply in debt. The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company was founded in 1898 by Frank Seiberling, who named it in his honour.

sec.t:
Long before Europe, people in Mexico and Central America knew rubber well. About 3,600 years ago, they mixed latex with juice from a morning glory vine, which made it bouncier. Scientists at MIT recreated the recipe in the 1990s and found it worked.

They used rubber for sandals, bands and solid balls, some weighing a few kilograms. The balls were for a game played in stone courts by the Olmec, and later by the [[@aztecs-maya|Maya and Aztecs]]. When Spanish visitors saw these balls in the 1500s, they were astonished. Nothing in Europe bounced like that.

In the early 1830s, Americans went wild for rubber. Factories made [[@raincoats-waterproof|raincoats]], boots and [[@life-jackets|life jackets]]. Then summer arrived. Coats melted, boots oozed, and the smell of rotting rubber filled warehouses. Customers threw their goods away and many rubber companies collapsed.

Charles Goodyear became obsessed with fixing it. He mixed rubber with almost anything he could think of, from magnesia to nitric [[acid|acid]]. He fell so deep into debt that he was jailed several times for unpaid bills, and his family sometimes went hungry.

Rubber is made of [[polymer|polymers]], very long chain [[molecule|molecules]] tangled like cooked noodles. When warm, the chains slide past each other, and the rubber flows. When sulphur is heated with them, it forms tiny bridges between the chains, linking them into a net.

Now the rubber can stretch, because the chains uncoil, but it snaps back, because the bridges hold. A little sulphur makes soft rubber bands. Much more makes a hard, black material called ebonite, once used for bowling balls and combs.

In England, Thomas Hancock studied samples of Goodyear's rubber and worked out a similar method. He patented it in Britain in 1843, a few weeks before Goodyear applied there. A friend of Hancock's suggested the name "vulcanisation". Goodyear spent years in court, and despite his discovery he died in debt in 1860.

Rubber trees grow wild in the Amazon. In 1876, the Englishman Henry Wickham shipped about 70,000 seeds from [[@brazil-amazon|Brazil]] to London. Seedlings went on to Sri Lanka and Malaysia, and plantations spread across Asia. Today most of the world's natural rubber comes from South-East Asia, and in India, [[@kerala|Kerala]] grows most of it.

Roughly half of all rubber used today is natural, and the rest is synthetic, made from oil. Most of both ends up in tyres. Rubber also lives on your desk: before rubber, people rubbed out pencil marks with bread, and the story of the [[@erasers|eraser]] began when someone tried a lump of latex instead.

text: Yes, planes can fly on electricity, but so far only small ones over short distances.

An electric plane uses batteries to power electric motors, which turn [[propeller|propellers]]. Electric motors are quiet, simple and cheap to run, and they don't give off exhaust. Several small two-seater electric planes already fly, and one, the Pipistrel Velis Electro from Slovenia, became the first fully electric plane to be type certified, in 2020, for pilot training.

The big problem is weight. Batteries store far less energy than the same weight of jet fuel. That makes it very hard to build an electric plane big enough to carry many people across a country, let alone an ocean.

st.prompt: A fuel-burning plane gets lighter as it flies. What happens to an electric plane's weight during a flight?

options.t: It stays the same, because empty batteries weigh as much as full ones
It gets lighter as the electricity is used up
It gets heavier as the batteries warm up

st.reveal: A jet can burn tonnes of fuel on a long trip and lands much lighter. Batteries don't shrink as they empty, so an electric plane has to carry their full weight all the way, which is one more reason long electric flights are hard.

NASA, X-57 Maxwell and electrified aircraft propulsion research.
n.certNote: Small electric planes already fly, and one is certified for pilot training. Experts disagree about how soon, or whether, batteries will be good enough for large airliners on long routes.

d.try: Make two paper planes the same way. Tape a coin to the nose of one. Throw both the same way several times and measure how far each flies. The extra weight is like a heavy battery, and it shows why designers fight for every gram.
myth: Electric planes can't fly yet. They are only an idea.

Small electric planes are already flying, training pilots and making short hops, especially in Europe. What doesn't exist yet is a battery-powered airliner that can carry hundreds of people a long way.

sec.t:
A kilogram of jet fuel holds about 12,000 watt-hours of energy. A kilogram of good lithium battery holds about 250 to 300. That is a gap of roughly 40 to 50 times. Electric motors waste much less energy than jet engines, which narrows the gap, but fuel still comes out far ahead, by something like 15 to 20 times.

That matters hugely in the air, because a plane has to lift everything it carries. A jet airliner flying from Delhi to New York carries well over 100 tonnes of fuel. A battery with the same usable energy would weigh far too much to get off the ground.

There's another catch. A fuel-burning plane gets lighter as it burns fuel, so landing is easier. An electric plane lands carrying the full weight of its empty [[@batteries-future|batteries]].

One of the most famous electric planes didn't need a charging point at all. Solar Impulse 2, a Swiss plane, had over 17,000 [[@solar-panels|solar cells]] spread across wings wider than a jumbo jet's. By day they powered four motors and charged batteries. At night the batteries kept it flying.

Between 2015 and 2016 it flew right around the world in stages, carrying one pilot at a time. In March 2015 it stopped in Ahmedabad and Varanasi. One leg, from Japan to Hawaii, lasted almost five days and nights without landing.

The plane was very light and very slow, often around 70 km/h, slower than a car on a highway. It proved what sunlight could do, but no airline could carry passengers that way.

{{story:wright-brothers}}

Where electric planes make most sense is short trips with few passengers. Training flights usually last under an hour and return to the same airfield, which suits batteries well. Flying schools in Europe now use electric trainers, which are cheap to run and much quieter than old [[piston|piston]] planes.

Other companies are testing small electric planes for short routes, such as hops between islands or nearby cities. In 2019 a Canadian airline, Harbour Air, flew a small seaplane with an electric motor in Vancouver. In 2022 an American nine-seat electric plane called Alice made its first flight.

Air taxis that take off straight up, sometimes called [[@flying-cars|flying cars]], also run on batteries and are designed for trips across a city.

For bigger planes, many engineers think the answer is a mix. Hybrid planes could use electric motors for take-off, when the most power is needed, and fuel engines for cruising. Others are testing hydrogen, which can power fuel cells that make electricity on board.

Flying produces a few percent of the gases warming the planet, and that share is growing as more people fly. That is why governments and companies are spending money on cleaner aircraft to slow [[@climate-change|climate change]]. For now, though, if you board a plane from Mumbai to London, it will run on kerosene for years to come.

text: Yes, hydrogen can power vehicles, and some already run on it. Most use a fuel cell, a device that combines hydrogen with oxygen from the air to make electricity. That electricity drives a motor, just like in a battery electric car. The only waste is water and some heat.

The hard part is the hydrogen itself. Almost all of it today is made from natural gas, which releases [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Clean "green" hydrogen, made using solar or wind power, is still expensive. So whether hydrogen will fill the roads, or mostly power trucks, ships and factories, is a real debate.

st.prompt: A hydrogen fuel cell car makes electricity from hydrogen and oxygen. What comes out of its exhaust pipe?
st.reveal: Inside the fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen from the air combine to make water, releasing electricity on the way. Hydrogen cars drip a little water instead of giving off fumes.

src: International Energy Agency, Global Hydrogen Review.
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Government of India, National Green Hydrogen Mission.
n.certNote: Hydrogen vehicles already work. Experts disagree about how big a part they will play, because making clean hydrogen is costly and batteries are improving fast. Many think hydrogen suits heavy trucks, ships, steelworks and some trains better than small cars.

d.try: Look at a plastic water bottle and read "H₂O" in your head. It means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen. Draw the molecule with two small circles stuck to one big one. Then draw what happens in a fuel cell, where hydrogen and oxygen join up to make water, and label where the electricity comes out.
myth: Hydrogen cars are dangerous bombs on wheels, like the Hindenburg airship.

Hydrogen catches fire easily, but car tanks are thick carbon-fibre cylinders tested in crashes and fires. Hydrogen is very light, so if it leaks it rises and spreads away quickly instead of pooling under the car like petrol.

up to about 700 times normal air pressure

sec.t:
A fuel cell has two sides separated by a thin sheet. Hydrogen goes in one side. A [[catalyst|catalyst]], often platinum, splits the hydrogen into [[proton|protons]] and [[electron|electrons]]. The sheet lets only protons through. The electrons have to go the long way round, through a wire, and that flow is electricity.

On the other side, the protons and electrons meet oxygen from the air and join up to make water. Nothing burns. There's no [[combustion|combustion]], just a steady chemical reaction, which is why fuel cells are quiet.

In September 2018, two hydrogen trains called the Coradia iLint began carrying passengers in Lower Saxony, Germany. They replaced diesel trains on a line without overhead electric wires. Since then, trains like these have run in a few other countries, though some German operators later chose battery trains instead because they cost less to run.

India has been working on its own. Indian Railways has built a hydrogen train meant for a route in Haryana, as a test for lines where putting up electric wires is hard, such as heritage hill railways. Most of [[@indian-railways|India's railways]] are already electric, so hydrogen is aimed at the gaps.

On Earth, hydrogen is locked up in water and in fuels like natural gas. Pulling it out takes energy. Most is made by heating natural gas with steam, which gives off carbon dioxide. Engineers call that "grey" hydrogen.

"Green" hydrogen is made by passing electricity from [[@renewable-energy|renewable sources]] through water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. In 2023, India launched its National Green Hydrogen Mission, aiming to produce 5 million tonnes a year by 2030, partly for [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] plants and refineries.

{{story:sun-what}}

The Sun itself runs on hydrogen, though in a completely different way: its core crushes hydrogen [[atom|atoms]] together in [[@nuclear-fusion|nuclear fusion]].

Here's the numbers problem. Turning electricity into hydrogen, squeezing it into a tank, then turning it back into electricity in a fuel cell loses more than half the energy. Charging a battery and using it loses far less, often around a fifth. For a family car, that makes batteries cheaper to run.

Hydrogen fights back on weight and refuelling time. A hydrogen tank fills in about five minutes, and the gas stores lots of energy for its weight. Cars squeeze it to about 700 times normal air pressure so enough fits on board. That matters for a heavy truck crossing a continent, a ship, or a plane, where batteries would be enormous.

Hydrogen is old news to rocket scientists. Many [[@rockets-how|rockets]] burn [[@rocket-fuel|liquid hydrogen]], chilled to minus 253°C, with liquid oxygen. ISRO's cryogenic engine, used on its GSLV and LVM3 rockets, works this way. Getting hydrogen into cars was always going to be harder than getting it into space, because a car needs a filling station on every highway. Only about a thousand hydrogen filling stations existed worldwide in 2024, most of them in Japan, [[@seoul|South Korea]], China and Germany. For now, the debate is as much about pumps as about engines.

text: Flag colours mean whatever the people who choose them decide they mean. There is no worldwide code. Red might stand for courage on one flag, for blood shed in a war on another, and for a revolution on a third.

Some countries write the meaning into law or official guides. Others leave it open, and people tell different stories about the same colours. Often a colour was picked because it was already on an old royal banner, a political party's flag or a religious symbol, and the meaning came later. Flags are a kind of shorthand. They pack a nation's history and hopes into a piece of cloth that a child can draw in a minute.

st.prompt: Purple is rare on national flags. Why?

options.t: Purple dye was once extremely expensive to make
Purple fades too quickly in sunlight

st.reveal: For centuries, the best purple dye came from sea snails, and it took thousands to dye one garment. Only emperors and kings could afford it. By the time cheap purple dyes appeared, most flag traditions were set.

src: Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, Flag Code of India.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, flag.
n.certNote: Some flags have official meanings written into law, such as India's. For many others, the meanings were added later or vary depending on who you ask.

d.try: Design a flag for your family, class or street. Choose two or three colours and one simple symbol, and write a short line explaining what each stands for. Then show it to someone without telling them the meanings and see if they can guess.
myth: The colours of the US flag have official meanings set by law.

No law gives them meanings. The idea that red stands for valour, white for purity and blue for justice comes from a description of the Great Seal of the United States written in 1782, not of the flag.

sec.t:
India's flag was adopted on 22 July 1947, just before independence. It is based on a design by Pingali Venkayya used during the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]]. It has three equal bands: saffron on top, white in the middle and green at the bottom.

According to the Government of India, saffron stands for strength and courage, white for peace and truth, and green for fertility, growth and the land. In the centre is a navy-blue wheel with 24 spokes, the Ashoka Chakra, taken from the Lion Capital at Sarnath, built by the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]]. It stands for the wheel of law and movement. For years the Flag Code required the flag to be made of hand-spun [[@khadi|khadi]], linking it to [[@gandhi|Gandhi]]'s freedom movement. In 2021–22 the rules were changed to allow machine-made and polyester flags too.

Red, white, blue, green, yellow and black fill most flags. One reason is practical. These dyes were cheap and lasted in sun and rain. Purple was the opposite. The famous ancient dye, Tyrian purple, came from sea snails, and making it was slow, smelly and costly.

Today only a couple of national flags include purple, such as Dominica's, which shows a purple-feathered parrot.

Neighbouring countries often share colours. Many African countries use red, yellow and green, colours taken from the flag of [[@ethiopia|Ethiopia]], one of the few African countries never colonised. Many Arab countries use red, white, green and black, from a flag flown in the Arab Revolt of 1916.

Many Muslim-majority countries use green, a colour linked with Islam. Pakistan's flag is green and white, with the white standing for religious minorities. Nordic countries, such as Denmark, Sweden and [[@norway-fjords|Norway]], all use a cross shifted to one side.

Nearly all national flags are rectangles. [[@switzerland|Switzerland]] and [[@vatican|Vatican City]] use squares. [[@nepal|Nepal]] is the only one that is neither, with two stacked pennants. Denmark's red flag with a white cross is often called the oldest national flag still in use, going back at least to the 1300s.

Studying flags has its own name: vexillology, from the Latin word for a flag.

text: Odisha is a state on India's east coast, facing the Bay of Bengal. It's famous for the Konark Sun Temple, the Jagannath temple and Rath Yatra at Puri, and the classical dance called Odissi. Its coastline is where huge numbers of olive ridley sea turtles come to nest.

It also has one of India's richest histories. The ancient kingdom of Kalinga was here. So is [[@chilika|Chilika]] Lake, where dolphins swim in brackish water, and hundreds of thousands of birds arrive each winter. And in recent years, Odisha has become known around the world for how well it protects people from [[cyclone|cyclones]].

st.prompt: In 1999, a super cyclone in Odisha killed around 10,000 people. When Cyclone Phailin, nearly as strong, hit in 2013, what happened?

options.t: Under 50 people died, because about a million were moved to safety in time
About the same number died, because nothing could be done
The cyclone turned away at the last minute

st.reveal: After 1999, Odisha built cyclone shelters, trained volunteers and improved warnings. When Phailin came, around a million people were evacuated, and deaths were far fewer. The UN and others praised it as a model for disaster planning.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sun Temple, Konârak.
Chilika Development Authority, Government of Odisha.

d.try: Fill a shallow tray with sand and bury a few marbles in a small hollow, the way a turtle buries its eggs. Smooth the sand over. Ask a friend to find them using only their fingers. Then think about how hard it is for predators, and for people counting nests.
myth: The wheels of the Konark temple are only decoration.
They are beautifully carved, but some of them also work as sundials. The shadow cast by the spokes on the wheel's rim can be used to tell the time of day.

sec.t:
The Konark Sun Temple was built in the 13th century, under King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga [[dynasty|dynasty]]. It was designed as a giant chariot for Surya, the Sun god, pulled by seven stone horses on 24 huge carved wheels. Each wheel is taller than a grown adult.

Some of the wheels work as sundials: the shadows of their spokes tell the time. The temple walls are covered with carvings of dancers, musicians, animals and daily life. The main tower has collapsed, but what remains is still enormous. In 1984, UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site.

sec.h: Turtles, dolphins and a giant lagoon
sec.t:
Olive ridleys are small sea turtles. On some nights, they come ashore together in vast numbers to nest, an event called an arribada, a Spanish word for "arrival". Gahirmatha and the Rushikulya river mouth in Odisha are among the most important places in the world for this. Weeks later, the hatchlings dig out and race for the waves.

Chilika Lake, south of Puri, is India's largest coastal [[lagoon|lagoon]], where seawater and river water mix. It is home to rare Irrawaddy dolphins, and to flamingos, ducks and other birds flying in from as far away as Siberia each winter.

Around 261 BCE, the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] conquered Kalinga, in what is now Odisha. The war was so bloody that, according to his own rock [[inscription|inscriptions]], he was filled with regret. He turned towards Buddhism and the idea of ruling through kindness. One of his [[edict|edicts]] is carved on a rock at Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar.

Odisha's art traditions run deep. [[@odissi|Odissi]] dancers use curved poses inspired by temple carvings. Painters in the village of Raghurajpur make [[@pattachitra|pattachitra]], detailed paintings on cloth, often showing Jagannath.

Odisha's long, flat coast is often hit by cyclones. In 1999, a super cyclone killed around 10,000 people. Afterwards, the state built hundreds of shelters, trained volunteers and planned how to move people fast.

When Cyclone Phailin struck in 2013, around a million people were evacuated, and the number of deaths stayed very low. Other states and countries have since studied what Odisha did. Each new storm still tests the plan, and each time the shelters along the shore fill with families waiting for the wind to pass.

text: In 1776, Philadelphia was the largest city in Britain's American colonies and the meeting place of the Continental Congress, a gathering of leaders from the 13 colonies. On 2 July, meeting in the Pennsylvania State House, they voted to declare independence from Britain. On 4 July, they approved the Declaration of Independence explaining why.

That building is now called Independence Hall. In 1787, delegates met in the same room to write the US Constitution. So, in the space of 11 years, one brick hall saw the birth of a new country and the rules it still runs on.

st.prompt: John Adams wrote to his wife predicting which date Americans would celebrate for ever. Which one did he pick?
st.reveal: Adams thought 2 July, the day of the actual vote for independence, would be the great day. But the date printed on the Declaration was 4 July, and that is the one that stuck.

src: US National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park.

d.try: Write your own class declaration. With friends, list three rules you think every class should follow and why, in short, clear sentences. Then have everyone sign it, one at a time, and notice how signing makes people feel responsible for it.
myth: The Liberty Bell rang out on 4 July 1776 to announce independence.
There is no evidence it did. The story comes from a made-up tale published in 1847. The bell may have rung with others on 8 July, when the Declaration was first read aloud, but nobody knows for sure.
facts: Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall

sec.h: A city on the edge of war
sec.t:
By 1776, fighting between the colonies and Britain had already begun, over taxes, trade and the right to govern themselves. Philadelphia, with around 30,000 people, sat in the middle of the colonies and was a busy port.

Delegates rode in from as far as New Hampshire and Georgia. They met in the State House through a hot, humid summer, with windows often shut to keep conversations secret. Flies from a nearby stable were said to bother them so much that they sped up debates.

On 2 July, Congress voted for independence. Adams wrote to his wife Abigail that the day would be celebrated with parades, games, bells and fireworks for ever after. He was right about the parties, wrong about the date.

On 4 July, Congress approved the final wording. On 8 July, it was read aloud to a crowd in the yard behind the State House. Most delegates signed a carefully handwritten copy on 2 August. John Hancock, Congress's president, signed so big that "John Hancock" became American slang for a signature.

The bell in the State House tower was cast in London in 1752 and cracked the first time it was rung in Philadelphia. Two local metalworkers, Pass and Stow, melted it down and recast it.

It was not called the Liberty Bell in 1776. Campaigners against slavery gave it that name in the 1830s, because of words cast on it from the Bible: "Proclaim Liberty throughout all the Land". The famous crack appeared in the 1840s. Today the bell sits in its own glass building, across from Independence Hall.

The Declaration says that "all men are created equal" and have rights to "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness". Yet many of its signers, including Jefferson, enslaved people. Women could not vote, and Native Americans were left out. Those promises were fought over for two more centuries, as the story of [[@slavery-freedom|slavery and freedom]] shows.

The ideas of 1776 travelled. When India's Constituent Assembly wrote the Indian [[@constitution|constitution]] in the 1940s, it studied the US Constitution, among others. Ideas like fundamental rights and courts that can strike down unfair laws found a place in it. B. R. Ambedkar, who led its drafting, had studied at Columbia University in New York.

In 2026 the USA marked 250 years since 4 July 1776, with celebrations across the country, including in Philadelphia. Every country marks its birthday differently, as you can see in [[@independence-days|independence days]] around the world.

text: Most linguists, the scientists who study language, say emoji are not a language on their own. A language needs grammar: rules for putting signs together to say new, exact things, like "the dog the cat chased yesterday ran away". Emoji can't do that reliably.

But emoji are not meaningless either. Many researchers say they work like the gestures and facial expressions we use when we speak. A smile, a shrug or a thumbs-up adds tone to words. Emoji do the same job in text, where nobody can see your face.

st.prompt: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs started as pictures, much like emoji. Why did they become a full writing system when emoji have not?

options.t: Many hieroglyphs came to stand for sounds, so they could spell any word
Egyptians had more pictures than we do

st.reveal: Hieroglyphs mixed pictures with signs for sounds, so scribes could write names, verbs and whole sentences. Emoji mostly stand for things and feelings, so they cannot spell out a new word.

n.certNote: Most linguists say emoji are not a full language, because they lack grammar and cannot express everything words can. Some researchers argue they behave like gestures or a new kind of writing, so the debate is open.

myth: Emoji mean the same thing to everyone everywhere.
Meanings shift between countries, age groups and even phone brands. A folded-hands emoji can mean "please", "thank you", "praying" or a high five, depending on who sends it.

sec.t:
In 1999, a Japanese designer named Shigetaka Kurita drew 176 small pictures for a mobile phone service. Each was just 12 by 12 dots. There were weather symbols, hearts, faces and a few objects. The word *emoji* is Japanese for "picture" plus "character". It has nothing to do with the English word "emotion", though the match is a happy accident.

In 2010, emoji were added to Unicode, the standard that lets every computer and phone agree on letters and symbols. That made them spread worldwide. By 2025, Unicode listed nearly 4,000 emoji, counting different skin tones. New ones arrive every year after a long application process, and anyone can propose one. Proposals must show that lots of people would actually use the new emoji, and most are turned down.

sec.h: More like a wink than a word
sec.t:
Writer and linguist Gretchen McCulloch compares emoji to gestures. When you say "great" with a sigh and rolled eyes, your face changes the meaning. Text can't roll its eyes, so we add a face. A single emoji can turn "fine" from cheerful into annoyed.

Just like gestures, emoji change from place to place. The thumbs-up is friendly in India and the USA but rude in a few other countries. Younger people sometimes use the skull emoji to mean "I'm laughing so hard I died", while older people may read it as a threat.

History shows how pictures can grow into writing. Egyptian [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and early [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]] both started as pictures of things. Over time, many signs began to stand for sounds or ideas, until people could write anything they could say.

Could emoji travel the same road? Some experts think a few emoji already act like words, such as the fire emoji meaning "excellent". Others say there is no sign of a real grammar forming. One brave fan even "translated" the whole novel *Moby-Dick* into emoji, with the help of hundreds of online helpers. Readers agree it is hard to follow without the original beside it.

Still, people have been adding pictures to messages since long before phones. Thousands of years ago, the first signs scratched on clay were little drawings too. The story of how humans got from those pictures to alphabets is the story of how [[@writing-began|writing began]]. Meanwhile, deaf communities have built [[@sign-language|sign languages]] with grammar as rich as Hindi or English, made entirely of hand shapes, faces and movement.

text: Honey starts as [[nectar|nectar]], a thin, sugary liquid that flowers make to attract insects. A honeybee sucks it up with her tongue and stores it in a special stomach called a honey crop. Back at the hive, she passes it mouth to mouth to younger [[@pollinators|bees]].

Along the way, an [[enzyme|enzyme]] the bees add splits the nectar's sugar into two simpler sugars, glucose and fructose. The bees spread the liquid into [[@candles|wax]] cells and fan it with their wings until most of the water has evaporated. When it is thick and sticky, they cap the cells with wax. That stored food is honey, and it feeds the colony through cold or rainy seasons when no flowers bloom.

st.prompt: How do bees turn runny nectar into thick honey?

options.t: They fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates
They mix it with wax to thicken it
They freeze it overnight in the hive

st.reveal: Nectar is mostly water. Bees spread it thinly in wax cells and beat their wings to blow warm air over it. Once it is thick enough, they seal each cell with a wax cap.
