sec.t:
Honey keeps for a very long time. It has so little water and so much sugar that [[bacteria|bacteria]] and moulds can't grow in it. It is also slightly acidic, and an enzyme from the bees slowly produces tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide, which fights germs.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old. Egyptians used honey in food, in [[@oddity-old-medicine|medicine]] and as offerings to their gods.

People have collected honey from wild bees for at least 8,000 years. A rock painting in a cave near Valencia in Spain shows a person climbing ropes to reach a bees' nest, with bees buzzing around. It is among the oldest [[@cave-art|cave paintings]] of people gathering food.

In India, honey hunting is still practised. In the Sundarbans mangrove forest of West Bengal, collectors called mouals go into the forest each spring to gather wild honey, facing danger from tigers. In the Nilgiri hills, people of several Indigenous communities climb cliffs on rope ladders to reach the giant nests of rock bees.

India has several kinds of honeybees. The giant rock bee builds huge single combs hanging from cliffs, trees and even water tanks in cities. The smaller Indian honeybee nests in hollows and is kept by farmers in wooden boxes. The European honeybee, brought to India in the 20th century, is now widely kept too.

The colour and taste of honey depend on the flowers. Honey from litchi orchards in Bihar is pale and fragrant. Honey from the forests of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] can be dark and strong. In the USA, clover honey is common, and orange blossom honey comes from Florida and California.

Honey was the main sweetener in many parts of the world long before [[@sugar|sugar]] became cheap. It sweetens tea and lemon water, and is a favourite home remedy for a sore throat.

There is one important rule. Babies under one year old should never be given honey, because it can carry spores of a germ that their young stomachs can't yet handle. For older children and adults, it is a safe and very old treat.

text: Yes, people have eaten seaweed for thousands of years, especially in East Asia. In Japan, Korea and China it is part of daily meals: wrapped around rice, floated in soup, or tossed in salads. Coastal people in Wales, Ireland, Hawaii and Chile have long eaten it too.

Most people in India and the United States eat seaweed without knowing it. Thickeners made from seaweed go into ice cream, chocolate milk, jelly sweets and even toothpaste. And the jelly called China grass, used in Indian puddings and falooda, is made from red seaweed. Seaweed is a kind of [[algae|algae]], simple living things that make food from sunlight.

sec.h: Nori and the Mother of the Sea
sec.t:
The best-known seaweed food is nori, the paper-thin sheets wrapped around [[@sushi|sushi]]. Nori is made by chopping a red seaweed, spreading it on frames and drying it, a bit like making handmade paper.

For centuries Japanese farmers grew it on nets in shallow bays, but nobody knew where the young seaweed came from each season. When harvests failed in the late 1940s, the industry was in trouble. Then in 1949 a British scientist, Kathleen Drew-Baker, found that the seaweed spends part of its life as tiny threads living inside old seashells. Japanese scientists used her work to grow baby nori in tanks. The harvest recovered. Today a monument stands to her in Uto, in southern Japan, and she is remembered there as the "Mother of the Sea".

Along the coast of Tamil Nadu, near Rameswaram and the Gulf of Mannar, women have collected seaweed for generations. Many dive from small boats, holding their breath, and pull seaweed from rocks on the seabed. Much of it is sold to factories that make agar and other products.

India also farms seaweed. Farmers tie pieces of seaweed to ropes hung from bamboo rafts in the sea, and harvest them after about six weeks. The government has been encouraging this as a way for fishing villages to earn more. In 2022 China grew far more farmed seaweed than any other country, according to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization.

Several seaweeds give us gels. Agar, from red seaweeds, sets firmly and is used in sweets and in laboratories, where scientists grow [[bacteria|bacteria]] on it. Carrageenan helps keep chocolate milk smooth. Alginate, from brown kelp, thickens sauces and [[@ice-cream|ice cream]].

If you read a food label and see one of these names, you are eating a little bit of the ocean.

Seaweed doesn't need fresh water, [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] or farmland. Giant kelp, which grows in [[@kelp-forests|kelp forests]] off California, can grow more than 30 cm in a single day. For this reason, scientists are studying seaweed as a food that could help feed more people without clearing land.

Seaweed is rich in minerals, especially iodine, which the body needs in small amounts. It can contain too much iodine if eaten in large amounts, so in places where it is eaten every day, people tend to eat small portions. A sheet of nori on your rice is fine. A whole bowl of kelp every meal would not be.

text: Yes, to a [[botanist|botanist]] a tomato is a fruit. It grows from a flower and holds the plant's seeds, which is the scientific test. It is even a [[@berries|kind of berry]].

But in the kitchen, almost everyone treats it as a vegetable. It goes into salads, curries and sauces, not fruit salad. In 1893, this difference ended up in the US Supreme Court. Both answers are right, depending on whether you are a scientist or a cook.

st.prompt: In 1893, the US Supreme Court ruled on whether tomatoes were fruits or vegetables. What did it decide?

options.t: Vegetable, because that's how people cook and eat them

st.reveal: The judges agreed that botanically a tomato is a fruit. But tax law used words in their everyday sense, and people serve tomatoes with dinner, not as dessert. So for taxes, it was a vegetable.

myth: Tomatoes have always been part of Indian and Italian cooking.
Tomatoes come from the Americas and reached Europe only in the 1500s. Italians took a long time to cook with them, and in India they became common only in the last two hundred years or so.

sec.t:
Wild tomatoes still grow in the dry valleys of [[@peru|Peru]] and Ecuador. They are tiny, about the size of a pea or a cherry. People in what is now Mexico farmed them and bred bigger kinds. The Aztec word *tomatl* gave us the name "tomato".

When Spanish soldiers conquered the [[@aztecs-maya|Aztec]] capital in 1521, they found tomatoes in its markets. They took seeds back to Europe, along with [[@chillies|chillies]], [[@corn-maize|maize]] and potatoes.

The tomato belongs to the nightshade family, which includes some poisonous plants. Its leaves and stems really do contain mildly toxic chemicals. So many Europeans grew tomatoes only as decorative plants at first.

In 1544, an Italian writer named Pietro Andrea Mattioli described the tomato. About ten years later he gave a yellow kind the name *pomi d'oro*, golden apples. That's why the Italian word for tomato is still *pomodoro*. Even so, [[@food-ketchup-history|tomato sauce]] didn't become common in Italian cooking until the late 1600s and 1700s. Today the tomato and [[@pizza|pizza]] seem inseparable.

The Portuguese and British brought tomatoes to India, probably in the 1600s or 1700s. For a long time they were grown mainly for European residents. In Bengal they got the name *bilati begun*, foreign brinjal, because the plants look a little like brinjal plants.

Only in the 1800s and 1900s did tomatoes enter everyday Indian cooking. Now they are everywhere: in dal tadka, in rasam, in [[@punjabi-food|butter chicken]] gravy, in chutneys and in ketchup. India is the second biggest grower in the world, and the price of tomatoes makes national news when bad weather spoils the crop.

A green tomato is full of [[chlorophyll|chlorophyll]], the same pigment that makes leaves green. As it ripens, the plant breaks down the green and builds a red [[pigment|pigment]] called lycopene, along with sugars and smells. Some tomato varieties ripen yellow, orange, purple or even striped.

Ripening is triggered partly by a gas called ethylene, which the fruit itself releases. Farmers often pick tomatoes while they are still pale and firm so they survive the trip to market. They finish ripening on the way, which is why a shop tomato and one fresh from a garden can taste so different.
